extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, students of poetry and readers of poetic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging poetic composition and poetic genius, drawn from a literary-critical essay (Biographia Literaria). Focuses on poetic object, form, imagery, diction, and signs of original genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to excite sympathy by faithful adherence to truth of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should have the power of exciting the sympathy of the reader by a faithful adherence to the truth of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted as one of two cardinal points of poetry (with novelty by imagination). The desirable effect is a realistic dramatic truth of emotions that arouses sympathy; used to justify subjects drawn from ordinary life as well as supernatural situations rendered 'real' by faithful emotional portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to give novelty through the modifying colours of imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should have the power of giving the interest of novelty by the modifying colours of imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty is achieved by imaginative treatment — accidents of light and shade, moonlight or sunset over familiar landscapes show how both adherence to nature and novelty can combine. This is the second cardinal point paired with sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-poem plan: supernatural/romantic vs ordinary life
rubrics_metrics.description: A deliberate compositional plan distinguishing two sorts of poems: (1) those whose incidents/agents are supernatural or romantic aiming to interest affections by dramatic truth; (2) those drawn from ordinary life aiming to awaken attention to daily loveliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an organizing principle (as in Lyrical Ballads). The supernatural poems require believable dramatic emotion; ordinary-life poems should transfer human interest from inward nature and awaken perception dulled by custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic faith — willing suspension of disbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry often depends on 'that willing suspension of disbelief for the moment' (poetic faith) to accept supernatural or unusual agents so long as human interest and truth are preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supernatural elements can be effective provided the emotions and dramatic truth are convincing; poetic faith is what allows readers to engage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of real life / ordinary language as a legitimate poetic style
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument (as proposed by Wordsworth) that the language of ordinary life (colloquial diction) may be used in poetry to produce pleasurable interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge records the proposal and controversy: the style should be defensible and adapted to purpose. He objects to over-extending the claim but acknowledges the experiment (Lyrical Ballads) of using ordinary language; notes disagreement where Wordsworth seemed to advocate this style broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a poem: immediate object is pleasure, not truth
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem (in the strict sense) is a composition whose immediate object is pleasure, not truth; it is distinguished from works of science or history by this object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems must also be discriminated from other pleasurable species (novels, romances) by proposing delight from the whole compatible with distinct gratification from each component part. The ultimate end may include truth or moral/intellectual effects, but the immediate purpose is pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual support of parts — unity and harmonizing of components
rubrics_metrics.description: In a legitimate poem, the parts must mutually support and explain each other; each component should harmonize with and support the purpose and metrical arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid poems made of isolated striking lines that absorb attention from context, and avoid unsustained compositions that leave only a rapid general result. The whole should be a balanced, harmonious unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct gratification from each component part
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem should produce such delight from the whole as is compatible with a distinct gratification from each component part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meter and recurring sound patterns require that each part justify the attention it receives; if metre is present, every component must contribute to the overall pleasure and be worth attending to individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader engagement should be by pleasurable activity, not mere curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader should be carried forward by the pleasurable activity of mind excited by attractions of the journey itself rather than merely by curiosity or restless desire for a final solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge uses metaphors (serpent motion, path of sound) to stress sustained, pleasurable intellectual motion. Effective poetry invites active mental engagement throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studied selection and artificial arrangement to keep non-poetic parts in keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer compositions that are not 'all poetry' require studied selection and artificial arrangement so remaining prose-like parts partake of the poem's unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To preserve a harmonious whole, non-poetic sections must be chosen and arranged so they do not break the overall poetic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical arrangement must justify attention to recurring sounds
rubrics_metrics.description: If metre (with or without rhyme) is superadded to a composition, all other parts must be consonant with it and justify the perpetual and distinct attention to sound recurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metre is not mere ornament: the content must be adapted so that metre's demands (recurrence of accent and sound) are meaningful and pleasurable rather than mechanical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetness and adaptability of versification
rubrics_metrics.description: Sweetness of versification — musical delight and adaptation of rhythm to the subject — is a mark of poetic excellence (especially in early work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variation in the march of words is valuable so long as it does not pass into loftier, majestic rhythm unsuitable to the thoughts. Original, not mechanically imitated, musical quality is especially favorable in young poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of subject remote from personal private circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: A sign of genius is choosing subjects remote from the writer's private sensations and circumstances; subject-matter drawn directly from the poet's own experience can be an equivocal sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When subjects are too close to personal experience, excellence may merely reflect autobiography rather than original poetic power; greater distance often reveals superior imaginative capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery must be modified by predominant passion or associated thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Images, however beautiful, become proofs of original genius only when modified by a predominant passion, associated thoughts/images awakened by that passion, or when they reduce multitude to unity or transfer human/intellectual life to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Shakespeare show that imagery becomes poetic when it participates in a controlling feeling or thought, thereby contributing to unity and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery should be molded to circumstances, passion, or character
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery attains higher worth when it molds and colours itself to the circumstances, passion, or character present in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare's plays are cited: imagery that adapts to character and situation gives dignity and passion to presented objects; this is superior to generic or detached description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and energy of thought (intellectual power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth and energy of thought are indispensable — no great poet has lacked profound philosophical capacity; poetry is the blossom of human knowledge and thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic genius combines creative power with intellectual energy; without sustained thought, poetic gifts result in only transient flashes. Shakespeare and Milton exemplify the reconciliation of imagination and intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of imagination: blending and reconciling opposites
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetic imagination reconciles opposite or discordant qualities (sameness with difference, general with concrete, idea with image, novelty with familiar, heightened emotion with steady judgment) producing a synthetic unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination, under gentle control of will and understanding, blends elements into a single tone and spirit; this synthetic power is core to poetic genius and guides subordinating art to nature and manner to matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid novelty as mere novelty; value in superior manner of treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should avoid seeking novelty for its own sake; excellence may lie in superior manner of treating established subjects rather than in exotic new subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge contrasts modern tendencies to chase striking new images with earlier masters (Italian/Flemish) who achieved distinction by treatment, finish, and appropriateness rather than novelty alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity and fidelity of diction — guard the native tongue
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet should guard the purity of his native language: avoid meretricious, over-worn diction or words unfit for dignified expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge praises simplicity and appropriateness, invoking Dante's duty to preserve a language. Language is the armory of the human mind; careless or affected diction undermines poetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and subtle balance of sound within common metres
rubrics_metrics.description: True metrical variety often arises from countless modifications and subtle balances of sound within common metres rather than from adopting new, mechanically overpowering metres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge criticizes mechanical metre or foreign tunes that demand a forced vocal emphasis, preferring nuanced internal tonal variety that contributes to meaning and harmony.
